ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The androgen receptor (AR) is a nuclear hormone receptor that mediates the effects of testosterone and dihydrotestosterone. Mutations or dysregulation of AR cause disorders ranging from androgen insensitivity to prostate cancer progression.

sections.p: AR is a ligand‑activated transcription factor located in the cytoplasm that moves to the nucleus when bound by testosterone or DHT. Diagnosis of AR‑related disease relies on clinical features, hormone levels, and genetic testing for AR mutations.
b: Immunohistochemistry shows nuclear AR positivity in prostate tissue
PCR or sequencing detects CAG repeat expansions in spinal‑bulbar muscular atrophy

sections.p: In prostate cancer, AR activity is staged by the TNM system and Gleason grade; in androgen insensitivity, severity is graded by external genital phenotype (complete, partial, mild).
b: Complete AIS: phenotypic female with XY karyotype
Partial AIS: ambiguous genitalia, variable virilisation

sections.p: AR dysfunction can be genetic (X‑linked AR mutations), acquired (over‑expression in prostate cancer), or pharmacologic (anti‑androgen therapy). In low‑resource settings, chronic infections (HIV, hepatitis B) can alter androgen metabolism and exacerbate AR‑driven cancers.
b: X‑linked AR loss‑of‑function mutation
AR amplification in castration‑resistant prostate cancer
Chronic hepatitis B increasing hepatic androgen conversion

sections.p: Patients may present with ambiguous genitalia at birth, infertility, reduced secondary sexual characteristics, or, in adults, progressive prostate cancer despite castration.
b: Primary amenorrhea in AIS
Progressive PSA rise in castration‑resistant disease

sections.p: Targeted tests clarify the role of AR in the presenting disorder.
b: If hormone assays are unavailable, use clinical signs (virilisation, muscle mass) and imaging to infer androgen effect.

t.b: Is androgen production adequate? Low levels suggest hypogonadism; high DHT with normal testosterone points to 5‑α‑reductase excess.
Is the tumour AR‑positive? Positive staining supports androgen‑driven prostate cancer; negative suggests neuroendocrine differentiation.
Is there a pathogenic mutation? Detects AIS or SBMA; a polyglutamine expansion confirms spinal‑bulbar muscular atrophy.
Is tumour activity rising? Rising PSA despite castration indicates AR‑mediated resistance.

sections.p: Unchecked AR signalling in prostate cancer leads to metastasis; severe AIS can cause gonadal tumours; SBMA may progress to respiratory failure.
b: Rapid PSA doubling time
Testicular mass in AIS
Progressive dysphagia in SBMA

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then modulate AR activity. Surgical gonadectomy removes tumour risk in AIS; anti‑androgens block AR in prostate cancer; hormone replacement restores function in hypogonadism.
b: Bicalutamide or enzalutamide: block AR ligand binding, preferred in castration‑resistant prostate cancer
Spironolactone: weak AR antagonist, used for acne and hirsutism, avoided in pregnancy
Avoid high‑dose steroids that up‑regulate AR expression

sections.p: Regular monitoring of hormone levels, PSA, and imaging prevents progression. In AIS, annual testicular ultrasound screens for malignancy. Counsel patients on fertility options and genetic testing for family members.
b: PSA every 3–6 months in treated prostate cancer
Ultrasound annually in AIS

sections.p: Conditions that mimic AR dysfunction include 5‑α‑reductase deficiency, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and estrogen‑dependent breast cancer.
b: 5‑α‑reductase deficiency: low DHT, normal AR
CAH: excess adrenal androgens, normal AR

sections.p: Serum testosterone may be normal in AIS because the receptor is non‑functional; PSA can be low in neuroendocrine prostate cancer despite aggressive disease.
b: Normal testosterone does not rule out AIS
Low PSA does not exclude AR‑driven cancer if neuroendocrine features present

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden rise in PSA, new bone pain, or neurological decline in SBMA
Rapidly enlarging testicular mass in AIS

faq.q: Why does DHT bind AR more strongly than testosterone?
faq.a: DHT has a higher affinity for the ligand‑binding domain, making it about ten times more potent in activating AR transcription.
They control growth by blocking AR but do not eradicate disease; resistance often develops.
No; complete AIS individuals live healthy lives as females, but need gonadectomy to prevent tumours.

exam: Explain how AR signaling contributes to castration‑resistant prostate cancer and list two therapeutic strategies targeting this pathway.
Describe the clinical features that differentiate complete androgen insensitivity syndrome from 5‑α‑reductase deficiency.
